Supporting children online: privacy, messages and what to do when something goes wrong

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Online conversations can be part of learning, friendship and everyday life before and during the teenage years. Parents may worry about who is making contact, whether a private message will be forwarded or how to help after an upsetting exchange. Protection involves more than checking a device: children need clear expectations, suitable supervision and an adult they can approach. Online harms are real, but fear, blame or a promise that a particular control guarantees safety will not provide a reliable plan.

Start the conversation before there is a crisis

Talk regularly about what your child enjoys online, who they communicate with and what has felt uncomfortable. Use language suited to age, understanding and communication needs. Younger children need closer practical support; older children still need involvement and accessible help as privacy and independence grow. School, friends’ devices and games can all be part of the picture, not only the phone used at home.

You do not need to be a technology expert to offer useful support. Ask the child to explain an app or game and look up reliable guidance together when needed. A short conversation during an ordinary activity, or a supportive text, may be easier than a formal interrogation. Keep another trusted adult available if the child cannot initially speak with you.

Balance privacy with explained, proportionate supervision

Agree what you will check, why it matters, what information will stay private and what circumstances require more direct action. Review the agreement as the child’s abilities and circumstances change. Routine secret surveillance or reading every conversation is not a substitute for trust, and wanting privacy does not by itself show that a child is in danger.

Privacy does not mean ignoring a concrete safeguarding concern. If you suspect exploitation, threats or immediate danger, act and involve appropriate professional support; explain what you are doing as safely as possible. Do not promise absolute secrecy about abuse. Tell the child that information will be shared only with people who need it to help. Regulatory duties on online services vary by country; they are not a universal rule that removes a parent’s responsibility to protect a child.

Take part without taking over their friendships

Ask about the people, groups and games that matter to your child. A family message thread or an occasional friendly text can help keep contact ordinary, but joining every group, impersonating a friend or demanding constant access is not necessary for connection. Ask how messages make them feel rather than requiring a transcript of every exchange.

Explore privacy, reporting, muting and blocking tools together in the services the child actually uses. Interfaces and rules change, so consult the service’s current help pages rather than relying on a remembered button sequence. Check applicable age requirements and local rules. Knowing how to ask for help matters even if access to a particular app is not allowed; a child who used it anyway should still be able to report harm.

Carry respect and kindness into messages and posts

Discuss how a message, photo or rumour can affect another person. Private chats can be copied, forwarded or shown to others, and a small group is not a guarantee of confidentiality. Encourage a pause before posting, especially when angry or under pressure, and permission before sharing someone else’s personal information or ordinary photos.

The responsibility for harassment or non-consensual sharing lies with the person doing it; a child does not deserve abuse because they trusted someone or sent a message. Do not circulate embarrassing content to teach a lesson, expose another child or warn a parent group. Model the same care yourself when posting about your child. Sensitive details about a child’s school, location, relationships or an incident should not become public material.

Use a family agreement and controls as part of the plan

Agree realistic expectations about contacts, sharing, purchases, privacy and when to ask before trying a new service. Explain controls and limits, involve the child in decisions they can understand and revisit the plan. The aim is a workable safety arrangement, not a promise that obedience will prevent every problem. Adapt support for disability, language or learning needs.

Controls can help manage content or features, but coverage differs between the device, app, account and network. A home broadband filter does not automatically cover a mobile connection or a friend’s WiFi, and no filter catches everything. Check current settings with the provider and discuss what the child should do when something gets through. Technical controls should support ongoing conversations, not replace them.

When the child tells you, help first and investigate calmly

Thank them for telling you, listen and ask what happened without starting with blame or punishment. Find out whether they are safe now, whether someone is threatening or pressuring them, and whether there is an urgent risk to them or another person. Do not require them to repeatedly describe distressing details or show an intimate image to prove the problem.

A calm response does not mean treating harm as trivial. Help stop further contact or sharing, use the appropriate reporting route and explain the next steps. If a household rule was broken, discuss it separately after immediate safety is addressed. Automatic punishment for disclosing a problem can make future disclosure harder. Avoid promising that nobody will find out, that removal is certain or that the situation will resolve immediately.

Respond to bullying and unwanted contact

Hurtful rumours, repeated abusive messages, impersonation and public humiliation can affect a child both online and offline. Do not dismiss this as harmless drama. A one-off threat, sexual request or frightening message can also need help even if it does not fit a repeated-bullying definition. The person making contact may be a peer, someone known offline or a stranger.

Where safe, note the account name, service, dates and relevant links or ordinary non-sexual text messages. Report harmful content through the service and use mute or block functions to reduce contact; do not encourage retaliation. Involve the school’s safeguarding or pastoral team when appropriate, and seek police or child-protection advice for threats, exploitation or serious concerns. Do not delay urgent help while assembling evidence.

If your child sent something harmful, stop the harm without public shaming

A child may have forwarded a rumour, sent a cruel message or shared someone else’s material. Be clear that harmful sharing must stop, while keeping support available. Ask what happened and whether pressure, coercion or another safety issue is involved. Do not assume that only boys send harmful messages or that only girls receive them.

Help them take responsibility through an appropriate, non-violent plan with the school or relevant professionals. Do not organize a public confrontation, circulate the content to other parents or demand direct contact with the affected child when that could cause more harm. If the material is sexual or involves a minor’s intimate image, use specialist safeguarding advice rather than treating it as an ordinary disagreement to settle by forwarding screenshots.

Handle evidence without making new copies of intimate images

Ordinary abusive text, usernames, dates, platform details and links may help a report. Keep these private and share them only through appropriate reporting channels. If a message includes a nude or sexual image, or a preview of one, do not take a screenshot that copies it. Do not download, record, forward or ask anyone to send a nude or sexual image of a person under 18, or whose age is uncertain, including to a parent for proof.

Tell the reporting service what happened and ask how to handle material already on a device. Police and specialist child-protection services can advise what information is needed and what to do about existing material; laws differ. You do not need a perfect record before asking for help. Before deleting an account in a panic, ask the investigating service about lawful evidence handling. Do not upload intimate images to BeMama, a chatbot, a parent group or an informal adviser.

Pressure, sexual exploitation or blackmail needs prompt specialist help

Requests for sexual images, pressure to livestream or meet, threats to share an image, or demands for money or more material are safeguarding concerns. Reassure the child that coercion and abuse are not their fault. Stop communicating with the person, do not pay or send more material, and obtain police or specialist child-protection advice. Paying does not guarantee that threats will stop.

Do not confront or try to trap the person yourself, and do not ask the child to keep engaging to gather evidence. If there is immediate danger, threatened violence or concern that someone cannot stay safe, contact local emergency services. A platform report, removal request or non-emergency online form is not an emergency response. Support the child while the incident is addressed, whatever choices led up to it.

Choose a reporting route that fits the incident and country

Start with the service’s reporting tools for harmful content, and contact local police, child-protection services or the school as the situation requires. Reporting systems have different purposes. For example, the UK’s CEOP deals with online child sexual abuse and grooming; it is not a general route for bullying, fake accounts or hacking. In Australia, eSafety’s serious child-cyberbullying scheme has residency, age and other eligibility requirements and generally requires reporting to the platform first.

Image-removal support is also available, with limits. NCMEC’s Take It Down can help with eligible intimate images taken before the person turned 18, including when they are now older. Use it only according to its official original-device instructions; never download an image or have someone send it in order to use the service. The UK-linked Childline/IWF Report Remove service supports eligible under 18s and involves the young person. Follow the official service guidance, not instructions from an unknown person offering to recover or remove images.

Removal tools cannot guarantee every copy disappears

Take It Down creates a digital fingerprint on the device rather than sending the image itself through that process. Participating services can use it on supported public or unencrypted surfaces; it does not cover every website or encrypted conversation. Report Remove also has assessment and technical limits. A report may help reduce circulation without guaranteeing complete removal or preventing every future upload.

Image-removal work does not replace reporting threats or abuse, and it does not remove the need for emotional support. Keep track of report references, the legitimate service used and agreed follow-up, without storing intimate material in a family log. If a service cannot help, ask an appropriate safeguarding professional about another route rather than repeatedly searching for or circulating the image.

Keep contact and support going after the immediate response

Check how the child is sleeping, feeling about school and relationships, and whether unwanted contact continues. Offer ordinary routines and connection without repeatedly questioning them or making the incident their identity. Seek professional help for persistent distress, withdrawal, loss of interest or difficulty functioning. Tell them they can come back even if the first report did not solve everything.

Get immediate professional help for self-injury or talk of harming oneself or someone else. Serious injury, possible overdose, immediate violence or inability to keep anyone safe needs local emergency services. Stay with the child if safe and involve another trusted adult. The person in crisis should not drive themselves to emergency care; arrange a safe driver or an ambulance. Review the family plan later, keeping privacy, safety and the child’s ability to seek help at its centre.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Agree clear privacy and supervision boundaries with the child, practise reporting and blocking on their actual services and revisit the plan as their needs change.

If something goes wrong, check safety and obtain appropriate help first. Record safe account, date and link details without copying or forwarding a minor’s intimate image.

Use official reporting and removal routes, check their country and eligibility limits and keep a follow-up plan. Do not wait for an online form or perfect evidence when there is immediate danger.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help note family agreements, report references, follow-up dates and questions for a safeguarding professional. Do not place intimate images, copied private conversations or unnecessary identifying details of children in it. It cannot investigate abuse, identify an offender, determine legal duties, remove content or provide an emergency response. Recording must not delay help.

When to seek help

For coercion, sexual exploitation, blackmail or serious threats, seek appropriate police or child-protection help promptly. Do not pay, send more material or confront the person. Never copy or forward a minor’s intimate image to prove an incident. Get immediate professional help for self-injury or talk of harming anyone; serious injury, overdose, immediate violence or inability to keep anyone safe requires emergency services. Stay with the child if safe, involve a trusted adult and arrange a safe driver or an ambulance; the person in crisis should not drive themselves to emergency care. A report or removal request does not replace urgent protection.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Regular, calm involvement can support safety without turning every private conversation into a surveillance task.
  • Teach respectful sharing and consent; private messages can circulate, but a child does not deserve abuse or blame.
  • Help first when something goes wrong, then review household rules separately from the immediate safeguarding response.
  • Record safe message/account details, but do not copy or forward intimate images involving minors for evidence.
  • Use legitimate reporting and removal services with their jurisdiction and limits in mind; immediate danger requires emergency help.

Frequently asked questions

I am worried about my child online. Where should I start?

Ask what they enjoy, who they communicate with and what worries them. Keep conversations calm and regular, agree understandable boundaries and explore current safety tools together. Concern should lead to practical support rather than risk minimization, panic or a promise that monitoring prevents every harm.

How can I stay involved while respecting privacy?

Explain age-appropriate supervision, what you will check and when a safety concern requires more direct action. Revisit the agreement as the child develops. Use ordinary check-ins, and suggest another trusted adult if they cannot talk to you. Do not demand copies of intimate images or assume every private chat is suspicious.

How should I react when an online problem happens?

Listen, thank the child for telling you, check immediate safety and act on threats or exploitation. Do not start with shame or automatic punishment. Help report harmful content and stop further contact or sharing where appropriate. Discuss broken household rules separately after safety is addressed; do not promise secrecy or guaranteed removal.

What is the best way to prevent online harm?

There is no guaranteed method. Combine a supportive relationship, age- and ability-appropriate boundaries, respectful sharing, current privacy settings and knowledge of how to ask for help. Controls have limits and cannot replace ongoing contact. A child should still receive help if an incident occurred after breaking a family rule.

Should my child send me the messages or pictures as evidence?

Ordinary non-sexual text and account details may be useful, but do not ask for nude or sexual images of anyone under 18 or whose age is uncertain. Do not download, screenshot, record or forward those images, including to yourself. Describe what happened to an appropriate reporting service and follow its instructions about material already on the device; do not delay seeking help for lack of a perfect record.

What if someone threatens to share an image unless we pay?

Stop contact, do not pay or send more material, and seek police or specialist safeguarding help. Do not confront the person or have the child continue the conversation to collect proof. Reassure the child that abuse is not their fault. Immediate danger or inability to stay safe requires local emergency services rather than waiting for an online report.

Will a report or removal tool erase every copy?

No service can promise that. Take It Down and Report Remove have eligibility, participating-service and technical limits; encrypted conversations and other sites may be outside their reach. Follow official instructions without making or obtaining new copies of a minor’s intimate image, and report coercion or threats separately.

When should we seek urgent help beyond a platform report?

Seek police or child-protection advice promptly for coercion, sexual exploitation, blackmail or serious threats. Self-injury or talk of harming anyone needs immediate professional help. Serious injury, overdose, immediate violence or inability to keep people safe requires emergency services. Stay nearby if safe, involve another trusted adult and arrange a safe driver or an ambulance; the person in crisis should not drive themselves to emergency care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
